When I was 19 years old, I raised my right hand and swore an oath to support and defend the Constitution of the United States against all enemies, foreign and domestic. I spent years teaching constitutional law to the next generation of Army officers at West Point.
I have taken versions of that oath more than once since then -- as a soldier, as a member of Congress, and while serving at the Pentagon. Over the years, I have thought a lot about why the oath is written the way it is. We don't swear loyalty to a president, a political party, or even the government itself. We swear an oath to the Constitution.
The Secretary's SitRep is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.
[Upgrade to paid](https://substack..pcxXJxg23xBhlsfDoTzO1Z1v1IgUKHa-LDOdrASL9bk?&utm_medium=email&utm_source=subscribe-widget-preamble&utm_content=213744017)
At 19, I understood what those words meant, but I don't think I fully appreciated their wisdom. Serving overseas as an Army paratrooper and prosecutor, then in Congress and later inside the executive branch, taught me what constitutional limits look like in practice.
The Constitution is more than the document that establishes our government. It is a living and breathing document that provides the blueprint, the architecture of American power. It determines how power is gained, how it is exercised, and where it stops. Because those rules are meant to outlast any one leader, the majority of citizens that might want to prey on a minority group, and it gives clarity to businesses and allies that they can have confidence that the United States will remain governed by institutions rather than by the whims of whoever holds office. At a moment of intense competition with China and Russia, that kind of predictability is a strategic advantage--and one we should not take for granted.
Much of the national-security debate today is about what America can build: artificial intelligence, energy infrastructure, critical-mineral supply chains and a stronger defense industrial base. All of that is important. But a country's strength also depends on whether its institutions can be trusted. Can our laws endure? Will our courts remain independent? Will political power change hands peacefully? America's constitutional system is directly tied to our national security.
Businesses invest in the U.S. in part because contracts are enforced by courts that do not answer to the ruling party. Entrepreneurs can build companies without needing political allegiance to the government in power as they do in China. Investors put capital to work with an expectation of predictable rules.
The same stability matters abroad. Allies make long-term commitments to the United States because they believe American institutions will outlast individual presidents. And our military can be trusted with extraordinary power because it answers to civilian authority and swears allegiance to the Constitution, not to the person temporarily serving as commander in chief.
That is a fundamentally different model from China's, where the Communist Party ultimately stands above courts, companies and other institutions. America's advantage comes from a system in which institutions are built to outlast individual leaders and political power is subject to limits. That stability gives businesses, allies and citizens more reason to trust the system--and that trust is a source of national strength.
That institutional infrastructure took centuries to build. We should be as serious about preserving it as we are about any other piece of critical national infrastructure. There are warning signs that we haven't been.
**The Trust Deficit - Only 10% Trust Congress to do Right By Them**
Only 17% of our fellow Americans trust the federal government to do what is right always, or even most of the time, in [Pew Research Center's 2025 measurement](https://substack.com/redirect/191d2e93-beb9-4f71-894e-c4dac2a800d5?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). [Gallup's 2025 survey](https://substack.com/redirect/6f99f184-b92e-4192-ae48-e4fb87fa974b?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) of major American institutions found confidence in Congress at just 10%. Confidence in the presidency was 30% and confidence in the Supreme Court was 27%.
One institution stood apart: the US military, at 62%.
There are many reasons Americans continue to hold the military in higher regard than most political institutions, and we shouldn't romanticize any institution or place it beyond scrutiny. But I believe Americans still broadly understand that the military is supposed to serve something larger than partisan politics. The uniform belongs to the country, and the oath belongs to the Constitution. It's one of the reasons why most military and military veterans are registered as independents.
Public trust is only one measure of institutional health. [The World Justice Project](https://substack.com/redirect/4c521d0b-ab1a-4280-84de-3b263e219fcb?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) found that the United States' score for constraints on government powers declined 15% between 2016 and 2023. [Freedom House](https://substack.com/redirect/46c1affe-63b9-4208-90f2-4bd52cd80ded?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)'s latest assessment gives the United States a score of 81 out of 100 for political rights and civil liberties, down from 84 the year before. And in April 2025, [Bright Line Watch](https://substack.com/redirect/5ce7edc5-663e-4af7-b97f-0e7ab0a67950?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) found that Americans rated the overall performance of American democracy at 49 on a 100-point scale, the first time the public's assessment had fallen below the midpoint since it began asking the question in 2018.
None of these numbers means the American experiment is ending, and I am wary of the overheated rhetoric that treats every political dispute as a constitutional crisis. Our institutions are stronger than that. But when independent measures of public trust, rule of law, and constraints on government power all move in the same direction, we should pay attention.
Executive power did not begin expanding with this president. Presidents of both parties have pushed the limits of their authority, particularly when Congress has been unwilling or unable to act. Congress, meanwhile, has spent decades surrendering some of its institutional muscle to the executive branch. Members of both parties have become far too comfortable changing their views of presidential authority depending on who occupies the Oval Office. That is political expediency and not fidelity to the Constitution they took an oath to support and defend.
An executive action that looks like decisive leadership when your party holds the presidency can suddenly look like dangerous overreach when the other party takes power. That is why the constitutional test cannot simply be whether you trust this president with a particular power. It is whether you would be comfortable giving the same power to every president who follows, including one whose politics, judgment or character you profoundly distrust.
**Half of Congress Has Been There Less Than Six Years**
I served in Congress as a Democrat, and I am proud of my record for two terms while both President Bush and President Obama controlled the White House. But I also served as an Army officer, where my obligation to the Constitution did not change with the party in power. Republicans should not embrace expansive presidential power simply because a Republican occupies the White House, and Democrats should not rediscover constitutional limits only when a Republican does. A principle that changes with the party in power is not much of a principle - it's more like political opportunism.
Congress has a central role in this problem. The Founders did not design the legislative branch to be an audience for the presidency. Congress writes the laws, controls federal spending, conducts oversight and holds major constitutional responsibilities over war and national security. Yet under presidents of both parties, it has repeatedly surrendered authority or failed to use the powers it already has.
We have seen the consequences of a muted Congress: silent as President Trump launched a war against Iran that has killed thousands and cost 18 American troops their lives, all without congressional authorization. Six months in, Congress still hasn't exercised its oversight role. Congress holds the exclusive constitutional power to declare war, and the 60-day clock under the 1973 War Powers Resolution expired months ago. Maybe now that they're back in session this week, they can dust off their copies of the Constitution and check out Article I, Section 8, Clause 11.
The same pattern has played out on tariffs, where lawmakers have delegated broad authority to President Trump to reshape trade policy with limited congressional involvement, even though the Constitution explicitly grants Congress the power to impose tariffs under Article I, Section 8 to "lay and collect Taxes, Duties, Imposts and Excises." (Historic terms for tariffs)
The political incentives are obvious. It is often easier to allow a president from your own party to act than to force 535 elected officials to negotiate their way toward a solution. But each time Congress chooses partisan convenience over institutional responsibility, the legislative branch grows weaker and the executive a little stronger. The next president inherits that imbalance regardless of party. One of the many reasons why only 10% of Americans believe Congress will do right by them.
**Power Corrupts and Absolute Power Corrupts Absolutely**
My experience in the military taught me something else about power: having the capability to do something is not the same as having the legitimate authority to do it.
The United States military possesses extraordinary power, yet it operates within an extensive framework of law, civilian control, congressional authority, rules of engagement and military justice. Those constraints don't make our military weaker. They are among the reasons its power is legitimate.
Checks and balances can sometimes look like frustrating obstacles to efficiency on cable television. But that friction is intentional. The Constitution was written by people deeply suspicious of concentrated power. They constructed a system in which different branches would compete with and constrain one another because they understood that even leaders with good intentions should not be entrusted with unlimited authority.
That can make democratic governments slower than authoritarian governments. But efficiency is not the same as strength, and that distinction matters enormously in our competition with China. As we say in the military, slow is smooth, and smooth is fast.
Beijing's argument to the world isn't simply that China has a large economy or powerful military. The Chinese Communist Party offers an alternative model of governance, one that can make long-term plans, mobilize resources and build quickly without elections, independent courts, legislative opposition or a free press standing in the way.
America should not respond by trying to become more like China. Our own history has shown that constitutional government can coexist with extraordinary economic, technological and military power. In fact, the limits on American power help make that power credible. Allies need to believe our commitments will survive the next election. Investors need to know that political leaders cannot arbitrarily rewrite the rules. And every time our institutions fail, our adversaries gain another example they can use to argue that democracy is unstable or obsolete. Weakening those institutions therefore carries a cost far beyond our domestic political fights. We are eroding an advantage our strategic competitors cannot easily reproduce.
That feels particularly important during America's 250th anniversary. I've spent much of my adult life wearing the American flag on my shoulder. But patriotism isn't about the size of your flagpole as I told CNN last week. It is about the people and principles that flag represents.

subject: Not a politician. A survivor, Peter
disclaimer_text: Paid for by John McGuire for Virginia
body:
| Peter, I wasn't supposed to make it this far.
Not after foster care. Not after my military service. Not after the day they told my family I wouldn't make it through the night.
But I'm still here. And if you've got 60 seconds, I want to tell you why.
I grew up bouncing between nine elementary schools, no name, no direction, just two grandparents who stepped in when no one else would.
I fought to survive back then. And that fight never really stopped.
At 18, I enlisted. Made it through BUD/S. Became a SEAL. Then a sniper. Then an instructor.
I carried out missions you'll never hear about. Buried teammates you'll never know. Stared evil in the face and pulled the trigger more times than I can count.
But in 2006, it all nearly ended.
A catastrophic injury. A doctor who looked me dead in the eyes and said, "You'll never walk again."
Most men quit at that point. But I didn't have that option. I crawled back, inch by inch, bone by bone. I stood. I walked. I ran. Then I never stopped.
My name is John McGuire.
And I'm not in politics because I wanted a title. I'm in it because I came back from hell and found my country being handed over to cowards.
Because the people trying to erase our history, mock our faith, and dismantle President Trump's legacy want 2026 to be their final victory, and they'll burn the rest of us down to get it.
They told me once I was finished. I didn't accept it then. I won't accept it now.

clean_body: | Peter, I wasn't supposed to make it this far. Not after foster care. Not after my military service. Not after the day they told my family I wouldn't make it through the night. But I'm still here. And if you've got 60 seconds, I want to tell you why. I grew up bouncing between nine elementary schools, no name, no direction, just two grandparents who stepped in when no one else would. I fought to survive back then. And that fight never really stopped. At 18, I enlisted. Made it through BUD/S. Became a SEAL. Then a sniper. Then an instructor. I carried out missions you'll never hear about. Buried teammates you'll never know. Stared evil in the face and pulled the trigger more times than I can count. But in 2006, it all nearly ended. A catastrophic injury. A doctor who looked me dead in the eyes and said, "You'll never walk again." Most men quit at that point. But I didn't have that option. I crawled back, inch by inch, bone by bone. I stood. I walked. I ran. Then I never stopped. My name is John McGuire. And I'm not in politics because I wanted a title. I'm in it because I came back from hell and found my country being handed over to cowards. Because the people trying to erase our history, mock our faith, and dismantle President Trump's legacy want 2026 to be their final victory, and they'll burn the rest of us down to get it. They told me once I was finished. I didn't accept it then. I won't accept it now. We just closed the books on August and another end-of-month fundraising deadline — and once again, this grassroots team stepped up when it mattered.

Look...I know I ask a lot of you. I know there are plenty of campaigns competing for your attention and your support. So when you choose to invest in this campaign and the work we're doing together, **I don't take it for granted.**

I got into public service because I believe people deserve leaders who show up, listen, and fight for them. That's what I've tried to do my entire career, and it's what I'm working to do every single day in Congress. Now, with the general election just a couple of months away, your support is helping make sure this campaign has what it takes to keep doing that work — and keep fighting for St. Louis.

There's still a lot ahead of us between now and November. **But today, I just want to say thank you for being in this with me.**

body:
What’s at stake for redwoods| | | [View in browser](https://click.everyaction.com/k/138361705/643841979/-909911469?utm_campaign=advocacy&utm_medium=email&utm_source=ea-news-all&utm_term=roadless-rule&sourceid=1170902&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9TVFJXTC9TVFJXTC8xLzg5NTc0IiwNCiAgIkRpc3RyaWJ1dGlvblVuaXF1ZUlkIjogIjIzZGYyOTdiLTMyYTYtZjExMS05YjMzLTAwMjI0ODJhOWE4ZCIsDQogICJFbWFpbEFkZHJlc3MiOiAiZHB3aWxsaXM2N0BnbWFpbC5jb20iDQp9&hmac=phtkF0_8xkdjmQaGundv1Qz44ngU7UNSsBG0vE-7FsY=&emci=ee2fbffd-b6a0-f111-9b33-0022482a9f1d&emdi=23df297b-32a6-f111-9b33-0022482a9a8d&ceid=1504551)

---
| | | Dear Peter,
---
You may have seen recent news that the U.S. Forest Service has proposed **[repealing the Roadless Rule](https://click.everyaction.com/k/138361707/643841981/1680156948?utm_campaign=advocacy&utm_medium=email&utm_source=ea-news-all&utm_term=roadless-rule&sourceid=1170902&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9TVFJXTC9TVFJXTC8xLzg5NTc0IiwNCiAgIkRpc3RyaWJ1dGlvblVuaXF1ZUlkIjogIjIzZGYyOTdiLTMyYTYtZjExMS05YjMzLTAwMjI0ODJhOWE4ZCIsDQogICJFbWFpbEFkZHJlc3MiOiAiZHB3aWxsaXM2N0BnbWFpbC5jb20iDQp9&hmac=phtkF0_8xkdjmQaGundv1Qz44ngU7UNSsBG0vE-7FsY=&emci=ee2fbffd-b6a0-f111-9b33-0022482a9f1d&emdi=23df297b-32a6-f111-9b33-0022482a9a8d&ceid=1504551)** , a longstanding national policy that limits road construction and most timber harvesting in designated roadless areas of national forests. Repealing this safeguard could open nearly 45 million acres of roadless National Forest System lands to roadbuilding and logging. The Forest Service says additional roads are needed for wildfire management. Yet [**fewer than 1% of wildfires in the lower 48** **states**](https://click.everyaction.com/k/138361708/643841982/875242130?utm_campaign=advocacy&utm_medium=email&utm_source=ea-news-all&utm_term=roadless-rule&sourceid=1170902&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9TVFJXTC9TVFJXTC8xLzg5NTc0IiwNCiAgIkRpc3RyaWJ1dGlvblVuaXF1ZUlkIjogIjIzZGYyOTdiLTMyYTYtZjExMS05YjMzLTAwMjI0ODJhOWE4ZCIsDQogICJFbWFpbEFkZHJlc3MiOiAiZHB3aWxsaXM2N0BnbWFpbC5jb20iDQp9&hmac=phtkF0_8xkdjmQaGundv1Qz44ngU7UNSsBG0vE-7FsY=&emci=ee2fbffd-b6a0-f111-9b33-0022482a9f1d&emdi=23df297b-32a6-f111-9b33-0022482a9a8d&ceid=1504551)**** have started in roadless areas of national forests. Research also shows roads can fragment forest ecosystems, increase erosion, and raise the risk of **[human-caused fires](https://click.everyaction.com/k/138361709/643841983/-806922034?utm_campaign=advocacy&utm_medium=email&utm_source=ea-news-all&utm_term=roadless-rule&sourceid=1170902&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9TVFJXTC9TVFJXTC8xLzg5NTc0IiwNCiAgIkRpc3RyaWJ1dGlvblVuaXF1ZUlkIjogIjIzZGYyOTdiLTMyYTYtZjExMS05YjMzLTAwMjI0ODJhOWE4ZCIsDQogICJFbWFpbEFkZHJlc3MiOiAiZHB3aWxsaXM2N0BnbWFpbC5jb20iDQp9&hmac=phtkF0_8xkdjmQaGundv1Qz44ngU7UNSsBG0vE-7FsY=&emci=ee2fbffd-b6a0-f111-9b33-0022482a9f1d&emdi=23df297b-32a6-f111-9b33-0022482a9a8d&ceid=1504551)**. Save the Redwoods is closely tracking this proposal. Fortunately, a repeal would likely have limited direct impacts on coast redwood forests, since most are outside the National Forest System. In the giant sequoia range, our analysis shows that most groves in roadless areas are generally protected by other conservation designations or are otherwise outside the scope of this rule change. However, roadless areas elsewhere in the Sierra Nevada and across the country could face increased risks if the rule is repealed.
---
---
This slope was once a logging road but now is a recovering forest. Removing roads like this reduces erosion, protects streams, and restores ecosystems. Photo by Max Forster.
---
This proposal stands in sharp contrast to **[our work](https://click.everyaction.com/k/138361710/643841984/-393852819?utm_campaign=advocacy&utm_medium=email&utm_source=ea-news-all&utm_term=roadless-rule&sourceid=1170902&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9TVFJXTC9TVFJXTC8xLzg5NTc0IiwNCiAgIkRpc3RyaWJ1dGlvblVuaXF1ZUlkIjogIjIzZGYyOTdiLTMyYTYtZjExMS05YjMzLTAwMjI0ODJhOWE4ZCIsDQogICJFbWFpbEFkZHJlc3MiOiAiZHB3aWxsaXM2N0BnbWFpbC5jb20iDQp9&hmac=phtkF0_8xkdjmQaGundv1Qz44ngU7UNSsBG0vE-7FsY=&emci=ee2fbffd-b6a0-f111-9b33-0022482a9f1d&emdi=23df297b-32a6-f111-9b33-0022482a9a8d&ceid=1504551)**. While federal policymakers consider opening more forests to road construction, we’re removing aging logging roads and restoring the streams and habitats they damaged. This slow, hands-on approach helps forests recover, function more naturally, and remain resilient for wildlife and communities. The Forest Service is seeking public feedback on the proposal through September 21. If you'd like to**[submit a comment](https://click.everyaction.com/k/138361711/643841985/347027800?utm_campaign=advocacy&utm_medium=email&utm_source=ea-news-all&utm_term=roadless-rule&sourceid=1170902&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9TVFJXTC9TVFJXTC8xLzg5NTc0IiwNCiAgIkRpc3RyaWJ1dGlvblVuaXF1ZUlkIjogIjIzZGYyOTdiLTMyYTYtZjExMS05YjMzLTAwMjI0ODJhOWE4ZCIsDQogICJFbWFpbEFkZHJlc3MiOiAiZHB3aWxsaXM2N0BnbWFpbC5jb20iDQp9&hmac=phtkF0_8xkdjmQaGundv1Qz44ngU7UNSsBG0vE-7FsY=&emci=ee2fbffd-b6a0-f111-9b33-0022482a9f1d&emdi=23df297b-32a6-f111-9b33-0022482a9a8d&ceid=1504551)** , feel free to adapt the language below: _"The U.S. Forest Service already faces more than $8.6 billion in deferred maintenance. Its limited resources would be better spent repairing roads, maintaining trails, and improving existing infrastructure than constructing new roads in wild landscapes."_ We'll continue to monitor the proposal and keep you informed. Thank you for standing with us to protect our redwood forests.

clean_body: What’s at stake for redwoods| | | | | | | | | | Dear Peter, You may have seen recent news that the U.S. Forest Service has proposed , a longstanding national policy that limits road construction and most timber harvesting in designated roadless areas of national forests. Repealing this safeguard could open nearly 45 million acres of roadless National Forest System lands to roadbuilding and logging. The Forest Service says additional roads are needed for wildfire management. Yet ** have started in roadless areas of national forests. Research also shows roads can fragment forest ecosystems, increase erosion, and raise the risk of . Save the Redwoods is closely tracking this proposal. Fortunately, a repeal would likely have limited direct impacts on coast redwood forests, since most are outside the National Forest System. In the giant sequoia range, our analysis shows that most groves in roadless areas are generally protected by other conservation designations or are otherwise outside the scope of this rule change. However, roadless areas elsewhere in the Sierra Nevada and across the country could face increased risks if the rule is repealed. This slope was once a logging road but now is a recovering forest. Removing roads like this reduces erosion, protects streams, and restores ecosystems. Photo by Max Forster. This proposal stands in sharp contrast to . While federal policymakers consider opening more forests to road construction, we’re removing aging logging roads and restoring the streams and habitats they damaged. This slow, hands-on approach helps forests recover, function more naturally, and remain resilient for wildlife and communities. The Forest Service is seeking public feedback on the proposal through September 21. If you'd like to** , feel free to adapt the language below: "The U.S. Forest Service already faces more than $8.6 billion in deferred maintenance. Its limited resources would be better spent repairing roads, maintaining trails, and improving existing infrastructure than constructing new roads in wild landscapes." We'll continue to monitor the proposal and keep you informed. Thank you for standing with us to protect our redwood forests. | | | With gratitude, Save the Redwoods League Top photo: Courtesy of Cal Poly Humboldt | | | Save the Redwoods League220 Montgomery Street, Suite 350 San Francisco, CA 94104 CONNECT WITH US | | | | | | ---|---|---|---|---|--- |

| Peter,

Every word in this letter comes directly from me, and I hope you’ll spare just a minute to hear me out.

Let me start off by saying the rising tide of socialism in this country should have real Americans terrified.

**First, it was Zohran Mamdani in New York. Then, it was Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan. Now, another Far Left socialist just won a Democrat Senate primary in Florida in a stunning upset!**

---|---|---
The workshop of Abna Fares Abu Zayed, a private generator company in the area of Al-Zawaida in the central Gaza Strip. August 2026. Photo courtesy of Mohanad El-Hemrawi.
NUSEIRAT REFUGEE CAMP, Gaza Strip--In the corner of a ground-floor room with a door that no longer closes, Emad Mahdi sits cutting nylon sheets into squares. Beside him is a pile of barbecue skewers, the kind sold for grilling meat. He glues the nylon to the skewers, ties them with thread, and leans each finished kite against the wall.
Mahdi, 60, is known in the camp as Abu Haidar. A photograph on the wall shows him holding a clothes iron, standing beside a friend. Both men are smiling. A crack from a nearby airstrike runs across the concrete wall.
Abu Haidar now makes kites for the children of Al-Nuseirat, although this was not his trade. The room where he now cuts and glues was once his dry cleaning shop, where he washed and pressed clothes for 37 years.
He stopped working when the war began in October 2023, but attempted to reopen his shop in early June 2026. "I opened the shop because I had no other way to make a living," Abu Haidar said. "But the electricity made it impossible."
The pressing boiler required 18 kilowatts to operate, many times what an ordinary household appliance uses. He bought electricity from a private generator company called Abna Fares Abu Zayed, paying 30 shekels (approx. $9) per kilowatt-hour.
Three hours of pressing cost him 800 shekels (approx. $240). He worked with one eye on the meter and the other on the iron. He kept his prices the same as before the war to attract customers but made little profit and on many days he found himself operating at a loss. Two months after reopening the shop, he was forced to close it again.
The four walls of the room now hold almost nothing except kites. All the machines are gone.
"First, I sold the boiler, then I sold the machine," Abu Haidar said. "Piece by piece, the business disappeared." After 37 years in dry cleaning, he had never expected to sell his equipment to feed his family. Unpaid electricity bills had piled up, taking more than half of what the sales brought in.
With no other source of electricity, he bought skewers and nylon and began selling what he could make without power.
Gaza has long suffered electricity shortages as a result of the Israeli blockade and successive Israeli assaults over the years, which have targeted the enclave's sole power plant and other electricity infrastructure. Yet since the genocide began in October 2023, the public grid has not delivered electricity to consumers, forcing Palestinians in Gaza to rely entirely on generators for power. Severe fuel shortages are a constant source of precarity, forcing the rationing of power but so far a complete shutdown has been avoided. But now, even the system of generators is threatening to collapse.
Fuel would eventually arrive in batches, and a generator could be restarted. Engine oil, lubricants, batteries, and the spare parts needed to maintain those diesel engines, however, have been another matter.
For the past 32 months, Israel has completely barred the entry of these materials, a ban that continued through nine months of the "ceasefire," according to the Palestinian Center for Human Rights (PCHR). Without oil and replacement parts, generators are wearing down from the inside and, one by one, breaking beyond repair.
Gaza's population had improvised a temporary replacement for the utility infrastructure destroyed by the war. Now, that replacement is itself nearing collapse. "We will reach a complete or near-complete shutdown," Mohsen Siam, spokesperson for the Generators' Owners Association, told Drop Site.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/cb407f0e-9c27-483a-bf08-b2c29b7872cf?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
The workshop of Abna Fares Abu Zayed, a private generator company in the area of Al-Zawaida in the central Gaza Strip. August 2026. Photo courtesy of Mohanad El-Hemrawi.
Before the war, Gaza drew around 600 megawatts of electricity; now, the amount entering the grid is zero.
Forty-eight of Gaza's engineers, technicians, and staff who kept the grid running have been killed in Israeli attacks since October 7, 2023, according to the Strip's Electricity Distribution Company. By June 2026, 85% of the distribution network had been destroyed.
Gaza's only power plant, located on the edge of Al-Nuseirat, has not run in more than two years. The Israeli occupation's bombardment cut the lines carrying electricity into Al-Nuseirat and throughout the Gaza Strip. Much of the camp's network still stands, though it is damaged and delivers no electricity.
In December 2025, the Gaza Electricity Distribution Company told residents of central Gaza not to expect power to return. Its crews were working on repairs, but the required materials had not been allowed in. According to Mohammed Thabit, the company's spokesperson, no equipment for the electricity sector has entered Gaza since the start of the war.
Gaza came to depend entirely on private generator companies like the one that supplied Abu Haidar's shop. Around 250 generator companies operated across Gaza before the war, according to Siam. Only 80 to 100 are still running, serving some 200,000 subscriptions covering homes, shops, institutions, clinics, and water wells. The rest have shut down for lack of oil and spare parts, Siam said.
Those still operating supply an average of 11 hours of electricity a day, though in some areas that figure has fallen to just three hours due to fuel shortages. Al-Nuseirat was one of them, and Abu Haidar's supply had dropped accordingly before he finally gave up and closed the shop in August.
## **Struggling to Keep the Generators Alive**
As Gaza's remaining generator network shrank, the electricity it produced became increasingly expensive, with prices rising tenfold. Before the war, a kilowatt-hour cost 3 shekels (approx. $1), Siam said, compared with 30 shekels now.
Even households using electricity only for lighting and charging phones now pay an average of 300 (approx. $100) shekels a month, according to Ahmed Abu Qamar, a Gaza-based economic researcher tracking local market data.
The price of engine oil also skyrocketed. A liter that cost 9 shekels (approx. $3) before the war had soared to around 2,000 shekels (approx. $675) by June 2024. Now, when it can be found at all, it costs about 3,000 (approx. $1,000). Spare parts, Siam said, are almost entirely unavailable.
Generator owners began pouring whatever they could find into their machines for lubrication: used engine oil strained through improvised filters, car oil, olive oil, and cooking oil.
The fuel was improvised too. When regular diesel stopped arriving, generator companies, including Abna Fares Abu Zayed, turned to locally made diesel produced by processing plastic waste in improvised furnaces. "We manufacture industrial diesel, and its cost is high, close to the price of Israeli diesel," Aya Shaheen, general manager of Abna Fares, said.
But the improvised fuel is expensive to produce, and it comes at another cost. No engine is designed to run on this Gaza-produced diesel. Mohammed Abu Alfa, maintenance manager at Abna' Fares, said the plastic-derived fuel clogs filters and injectors with thick sludge, and causes engines to produce black smoke and unusual noises. When heated, he said, its compounds become unstable and thicken into deposits that are acidic enough to corrode steel, aluminium, and the rubber seals in fuel pumps and injector lines. The fuel also ignites less readily than conventional diesel, resulting in incomplete combustion.
[](https://substack.com/redirect/a101fd95-cd75-466f-b704-fb8a74108863?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
###### Momen Abu Thuraya, the acting maintenance supervisor at the Abna Fares Abu Zayed workshop sprays a generator with diesel to wash off the residue of burnt engine oil. Al-Zawaida in the central Gaza Strip. August 2026. Video courtesy of Mohanad El-Hemrawi.
A damaged injector can leak raw fuel into the engine, washing oil from the cylinder walls and accelerating wear on the rings and pistons. The only remedy is regular oil changes, but that remedy is now beyond reach.
Several of Abna' Fares' generators have also gone permanently out of service during the war due to the absence of replacement parts needed for maintenance, Shaheen said.
In May, the company managed to secure a batch of engine oil on the black market. Yet the oil was of poor quality, and by May 30 the batch had disabled every generator the company operated. Service stopped completely for several days. Al-Nuseirat was one of the areas left completely without electricity during that period. While most of the generators eventually came back online, the Mega, the company's largest generator which runs at its Al-Nuseirat site, did not.
Israeli authorities classify electric generators and their spare parts as dual-use items, making their entry into the Gaza Strip conditional on special permits, according to the PCHR.
With replacement parts unavailable, the company began cannibalizing the generators it could no longer save. "The company moved parts from one generator to another, and bought from owners who had shut down their companies or closed their shops," Shaheen said.
## **" Attrition By Design"**
At Nasser Medical Complex, the same shortages risk life-threatening power failures. Of the hospital's four generators, only two are still running. The hospital requires 1,000 litres of generator oil a month, said Abdul Qader Karam Aliwa, a mechatronics engineer at the hospital.
The manufacturer specifies an oil change every 250 operating hours. Aliwa's team is now forced to stretch that to 1,500 hours. To replace the oil the engines burn through in daily operations, the team tops them up with used oil, causing friction between moving parts and damaging the engines themselves.
A generator without oil seizes and cannot restart even when diesel becomes available again. While a fuel shortage is a disruption, the damage caused by the ban on oil is permanent.
Two of the hospital's generators went out of service earlier this year for lack of oil and spare parts, shifting their load onto the two remaining generators and forcing them to run 12 hours each, providing electricity throughout the day. A year ago, three generators covered the load, running eight hours each. No spare parts for these generators are available on the local market.
In June 2024, one of the hospital's main generators failed at 2 a.m., cutting power completely for 15 minutes. Aliwa said they quickly received emergency calls for assistance from the intensive care unit and the neonatal incubators. Several outages have happened since.
Of the 111 generators serving hospitals across the Gaza Strip, 72 had broken down as of June, according to PCHR.
"What we are witnessing in Gaza is not a series of isolated shortages, it is a policy of attrition by design. For more than two years, we have observed Israel's policies restricting the entry of supplies. These policies do not merely delay aid; they dismantle the very systems people rely on to survive," Filipe Ribeiro, Doctors Without Borders' head of mission in Palestine said in a [report](https://substack.com/redirect/1ebaef31-dac8-47ad-a910-c9cf4fdbc2a9?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) earlier this month that found Israel's continued restrictions on engine oil and spare parts was increasing the risk of death and severe illness for thousands of Palestinians.
The electricity crisis is also affecting the livelihoods of thousands of Palestinians.
Muhammad Jabr worked as a tailor for 42 years before his workshop was destroyed. Now, at 64, he is displaced in the Hasayna area of Al-Nuseirat and has given up his generator subscription for the same reason as Abu Haidar: he could no longer afford it.
Without electricity, a sewing machine can be run manually, but Jabr immediately ran into problems. "Turning the wheel by hand means one hand on the cloth," Jabr said. "I cannot guide the cloth that way." A foot treadle leaves both hands free, but operating it all day was beyond what he could manage at his age.
Then his son Ahmed found a bicycle in the rubble of a neighbor's house. Its frame was rusted through, but the rear wheel and chain still turned. A local blacksmith welded it to an iron base pulled from the street and ran a rubber belt from the back wheel to the flywheel of the sewing machine.
The rust has never come off, and the wheel squeaks with every turn. Accompanied by this squealing, Jabr works from eight in the morning until the light fades, nine or ten hours, until he can no longer see. Nobody orders new clothes anymore. He patches trousers, alters donated aid garments to fit children in the camp, and replaces broken zippers. He works on thirty to 40 pieces a day, for one to three shekels each. On a good day, he brings in 30 to 50 shekels.
Jabr's 3-year-old grandson, Omar, even helps out. He is too small to reach the pedals from the seat, so he sits on the ground and turns them with both hands while his grandfather threads the needle.

August 2026. Photo courtesy of Mohanad El-Hemrawi. NUSEIRAT REFUGEE CAMP, Gaza Strip--In the corner of a ground-floor room with a door that no longer closes, Emad Mahdi sits cutting nylon sheets into squares. Beside him is a pile of barbecue skewers, the kind sold for grilling meat. He glues the nylon to the skewers, ties them with thread, and leans each finished kite against the wall. Mahdi, 60, is known in the camp as Abu Haidar. A photograph on the wall shows him holding a clothes iron, standing beside a friend. Both men are smiling. A crack from a nearby airstrike runs across the concrete wall. Abu Haidar now makes kites for the children of Al-Nuseirat, although this was not his trade. The room where he now cuts and glues was once his dry cleaning shop, where he washed and pressed clothes for 37 years. He stopped working when the war began in October 2023, but attempted to reopen his shop in early June 2026. "I opened the shop because I had no other way to make a living," Abu Haidar said. "But the electricity made it impossible." The pressing boiler required 18 kilowatts to operate, many times what an ordinary household appliance uses. He bought electricity from a private generator company called Abna Fares Abu Zayed, paying 30 shekels (approx. $9) per kilowatt-hour. Three hours of pressing cost him 800 shekels (approx. $240). He worked with one eye on the meter and the other on the iron. He kept his prices the same as before the war to attract customers but made little profit and on many days he found himself operating at a loss. Two months after reopening the shop, he was forced to close it again. The four walls of the room now hold almost nothing except kites. All the machines are gone. "First, I sold the boiler, then I sold the machine," Abu Haidar said. "Piece by piece, the business disappeared." After 37 years in dry cleaning, he had never expected to sell his equipment to feed his family. Unpaid electricity bills had piled up, taking more than half of what the sales brought in. With no other source of electricity, he bought skewers and nylon and began selling what he could make without power. Gaza has long suffered electricity shortages as a result of the Israeli blockade and successive Israeli assaults over the years, which have targeted the enclave's sole power plant and other electricity infrastructure. Yet since the genocide began in October 2023, the public grid has not delivered electricity to consumers, forcing Palestinians in Gaza to rely entirely on generators for power. Severe fuel shortages are a constant source of precarity, forcing the rationing of power but so far a complete shutdown has been avoided. But now, even the system of generators is threatening to collapse. Fuel would eventually arrive in batches, and a generator could be restarted. Engine oil, lubricants, batteries, and the spare parts needed to maintain those diesel engines, however, have been another matter. For the past 32 months, Israel has completely barred the entry of these materials, a ban that continued through nine months of the "ceasefire," according to the Palestinian Center for Human Rights (PCHR). Without oil and replacement parts, generators are wearing down from the inside and, one by one, breaking beyond repair. Gaza's population had improvised a temporary replacement for the utility infrastructure destroyed by the war. Now, that replacement is itself nearing collapse. "We will reach a complete or near-complete shutdown," Mohsen Siam, spokesperson for the Generators' Owners Association, told Drop Site. | | ---|---|--- The workshop of Abna Fares Abu Zayed, a private generator company in the area of Al-Zawaida in the central Gaza Strip. August 2026. Photo courtesy of Mohanad El-Hemrawi. Before the war, Gaza drew around 600 megawatts of electricity; now, the amount entering the grid is zero. Forty-eight of Gaza's engineers, technicians, and staff who kept the grid running have been killed in Israeli attacks since October 7, 2023, according to the Strip's Electricity Distribution Company. By June 2026, 85% of the distribution network had been destroyed. Gaza's only power plant, located on the edge of Al-Nuseirat, has not run in more than two years. The Israeli occupation's bombardment cut the lines carrying electricity into Al-Nuseirat and throughout the Gaza Strip. Much of the camp's network still stands, though it is damaged and delivers no electricity. In December 2025, the Gaza Electricity Distribution Company told residents of central Gaza not to expect power to return. Its crews were working on repairs, but the required materials had not been allowed in. According to Mohammed Thabit, the company's spokesperson, no equipment for the electricity sector has entered Gaza since the start of the war. Gaza came to depend entirely on private generator companies like the one that supplied Abu Haidar's shop. Around 250 generator companies operated across Gaza before the war, according to Siam. Only 80 to 100 are still running, serving some 200,000 subscriptions covering homes, shops, institutions, clinics, and water wells. The rest have shut down for lack of oil and spare parts, Siam said. Those still operating supply an average of 11 hours of electricity a day, though in some areas that figure has fallen to just three hours due to fuel shortages. Al-Nuseirat was one of them, and Abu Haidar's supply had dropped accordingly before he finally gave up and closed the shop in August. Struggling to Keep the Generators Alive As Gaza's remaining generator network shrank, the electricity it produced became increasingly expensive, with prices rising tenfold. Before the war, a kilowatt-hour cost 3 shekels (approx. $1), Siam said, compared with 30 shekels now. Even households using electricity only for lighting and charging phones now pay an average of 300 (approx. $100) shekels a month, according to Ahmed Abu Qamar, a Gaza-based economic researcher tracking local market data. The price of engine oil also skyrocketed. A liter that cost 9 shekels (approx. $3) before the war had soared to around 2,000 shekels (approx. $675) by June 2024. Now, when it can be found at all, it costs about 3,000 (approx. $1,000). Spare parts, Siam said, are almost entirely unavailable. Generator owners began pouring whatever they could find into their machines for lubrication: used engine oil strained through improvised filters, car oil, olive oil, and cooking oil. The fuel was improvised too. When regular diesel stopped arriving, generator companies, including Abna Fares Abu Zayed, turned to locally made diesel produced by processing plastic waste in improvised furnaces. "We manufacture industrial diesel, and its cost is high, close to the price of Israeli diesel," Aya Shaheen, general manager of Abna Fares, said. But the improvised fuel is expensive to produce, and it comes at another cost. No engine is designed to run on this Gaza-produced diesel. Mohammed Abu Alfa, maintenance manager at Abna' Fares, said the plastic-derived fuel clogs filters and injectors with thick sludge, and causes engines to produce black smoke and unusual noises. When heated, he said, its compounds become unstable and thicken into deposits that are acidic enough to corrode steel, aluminium, and the rubber seals in fuel pumps and injector lines. The fuel also ignites less readily than conventional diesel, resulting in incomplete combustion. Momen Abu Thuraya, the acting maintenance supervisor at the Abna Fares Abu Zayed workshop sprays a generator with diesel to wash off the residue of burnt engine oil. Al-Zawaida in the central Gaza Strip. August 2026. Video courtesy of Mohanad El-Hemrawi. A damaged injector can leak raw fuel into the engine, washing oil from the cylinder walls and accelerating wear on the rings and pistons. The only remedy is regular oil changes, but that remedy is now beyond reach. Several of Abna' Fares' generators have also gone permanently out of service during the war due to the absence of replacement parts needed for maintenance, Shaheen said. In May, the company managed to secure a batch of engine oil on the black market. Yet the oil was of poor quality, and by May 30 the batch had disabled every generator the company operated. Service stopped completely for several days. Al-Nuseirat was one of the areas left completely without electricity during that period. While most of the generators eventually came back online, the Mega, the company's largest generator which runs at its Al-Nuseirat site, did not. Israeli authorities classify electric generators and their spare parts as dual-use items, making their entry into the Gaza Strip conditional on special permits, according to the PCHR. With replacement parts unavailable, the company began cannibalizing the generators it could no longer save. "The company moved parts from one generator to another, and bought from owners who had shut down their companies or closed their shops," Shaheen said. " Attrition By Design" At Nasser Medical Complex, the same shortages risk life-threatening power failures. Of the hospital's four generators, only two are still running. The hospital requires 1,000 litres of generator oil a month, said Abdul Qader Karam Aliwa, a mechatronics engineer at the hospital. The manufacturer specifies an oil change every 250 operating hours. Aliwa's team is now forced to stretch that to 1,500 hours. To replace the oil the engines burn through in daily operations, the team tops them up with used oil, causing friction between moving parts and damaging the engines themselves. A generator without oil seizes and cannot restart even when diesel becomes available again. While a fuel shortage is a disruption, the damage caused by the ban on oil is permanent. Two of the hospital's generators went out of service earlier this year for lack of oil and spare parts, shifting their load onto the two remaining generators and forcing them to run 12 hours each, providing electricity throughout the day. A year ago, three generators covered the load, running eight hours each. No spare parts for these generators are available on the local market. In June 2024, one of the hospital's main generators failed at 2 a.m., cutting power completely for 15 minutes. Aliwa said they quickly received emergency calls for assistance from the intensive care unit and the neonatal incubators. Several outages have happened since. Of the 111 generators serving hospitals across the Gaza Strip, 72 had broken down as of June, according to PCHR. "What we are witnessing in Gaza is not a series of isolated shortages, it is a policy of attrition by design. For more than two years, we have observed Israel's policies restricting the entry of supplies. These policies do not merely delay aid; they dismantle the very systems people rely on to survive," Filipe Ribeiro, Doctors Without Borders' head of mission in Palestine said in a earlier this month that found Israel's continued restrictions on engine oil and spare parts was increasing the risk of death and severe illness for thousands of Palestinians. The electricity crisis is also affecting the livelihoods of thousands of Palestinians. Muhammad Jabr worked as a tailor for 42 years before his workshop was destroyed. Now, at 64, he is displaced in the Hasayna area of Al-Nuseirat and has given up his generator subscription for the same reason as Abu Haidar: he could no longer afford it. Without electricity, a sewing machine can be run manually, but Jabr immediately ran into problems. "Turning the wheel by hand means one hand on the cloth," Jabr said. "I cannot guide the cloth that way." A foot treadle leaves both hands free, but operating it all day was beyond what he could manage at his age. Then his son Ahmed found a bicycle in the rubble of a neighbor's house. Its frame was rusted through, but the rear wheel and chain still turned. A local blacksmith welded it to an iron base pulled from the street and ran a rubber belt from the back wheel to the flywheel of the sewing machine. The rust has never come off, and the wheel squeaks with every turn. Accompanied by this squealing, Jabr works from eight in the morning until the light fades, nine or ten hours, until he can no longer see. Nobody orders new clothes anymore. He patches trousers, alters donated aid garments to fit children in the camp, and replaces broken zippers. He works on thirty to 40 pieces a day, for one to three shekels each. On a good day, he brings in 30 to 50 shekels. Jabr's 3-year-old grandson, Omar, even helps out. He is too small to reach the pedals from the seat, so he sits on the ground and turns them with both hands while his grandfather threads the needle. | A guest post by| journalist, writer, and translator based in Gaza. clean_body: They are talking about the very real fear of watching everything we fixed, the border, the economy, our standing in the world, torn apart the moment the Socialist Democrats retake the House and turn Washington into a nonstop impeachment circus. | Peter, Everywhere I go in this district, people tell me a version of the same thing. At the grocery store, after church, at the gas pump, they lower their voice a little and say some form of the same sentence: “Please don't let them take it all back.” They are not talking about politics as a game. They are talking about the very real fear of watching everything we fixed, the border, the economy, our standing in the world, torn apart the moment the Socialist Democrats retake the House and turn Washington into a nonstop impeachment circus. I hear that concern, and I carry it with me every day I am in Washington. It is exactly why I refuse to slow down, even in the dead quiet of July. But I cannot wage this fight alone. I need people like you standing behind me. Beth Van Duyne | | PAID FOR BY BETH VAN DUYNE FOR CONGRESS

| | Good Afternoon,
Over the last several weeks, Rob has been busy across Northeast Pennsylvania and Washington, meeting with constituents, working with administration officials, and continuing to deliver for the people of the district. From engaging directly with local communities to advocating for NEPA’s priorities at the federal level, Rob has remained focused on getting the job done.
Just this past week, U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick visited the district alongside Rob to highlight the hardworking men and women who power Northeast Pennsylvania’s manufacturing sector. The visit provided an opportunity to showcase the strength of NEPA manufacturing and the important role local workers and businesses play in our economy. Rob continues to recognize the value union labor brings to the region and has earned the endorsements of 21 unions. As he continues fighting for Northeast Pennsylvania in Congress, Rob remains committed to supporting the workers, manufacturers, and businesses that create opportunity and keep our region moving forward.
---
[|
---](https://us.list-manage.com/TPCnavvdAbK?e=131e83a3c2&c2id=e7faf2081078228733221dbd5e122ac9)
|
---
| |
Recently, Rob welcomed U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy to Northeast Pennsylvania to tour the Nanticoke Bridge and the Wilkes-Barre/Scranton International Airport. The visit highlighted the importance of maintaining and investing in the critical infrastructure that keeps our communities safe, connected, and growing. Rob has already delivered significant federal investments for the Wilkes-Barre/Scranton Airport, securing $3 million for terminal facility upgrades and $18 million for Air Traffic Control upgrades. Rob will continue working to bring federal resources back to Northeast Pennsylvania and deliver real improvements for the district.
---
[|
---](https://us.list-manage.com/_YM8WvypbpK?e=131e83a3c2&c2id=e7faf2081078228733221dbd5e122ac9)
|
---
| |

Rob was also joined by Speaker of the House Mike Johnson for a press conference highlighting the stark contrast between Rob’s record and Paige Cognetti’s radical agenda. Speaker Johnson highlighted Rob’s strong support for law enforcement and praised his work ethic and commitment to the district. The two emphasized the choice facing voters between the common-sense leadership Rob brings to Northeast Pennsylvania and Paige’s left-wing Portland politics. Rob will continue standing up for law enforcement, putting public safety first, and delivering the common-sense leadership NEPA deserves.
---
[|
---](https://us.list-manage.com/uIdGrjnEFJD?e=131e83a3c2&c2id=e7faf2081078228733221dbd5e122ac9)
|
---
| | Rob recently was honored to receive the endorsement of the Christina-Doherty Fraternal Order of Police Lodge #84, representing law enforcement officers across southern Luzerne County. This marks Rob’s seventh FOP Lodge endorsement in Pennsylvania’s 8th District, along with the support of the Pennsylvania State Troopers Association. Rob has put in the work to make himself the right choice to protect Northeastern Pennsylvania.

_**Cliff 's Note:**_
##### David Shuster spent years as a correspondent at the networks, which means he has sat through the briefings, worked the sources, and learned exactly how careful you have to be with a story like this one. _**-- Cliff**_
* * *
_**by David Shuster**_
There is something terrifying these days about Vladimir Putin's predicament: after nearly five years of war with Ukraine, an estimated half a million Russian soldiers killed (plus another 1.1 million wounded) a crashed Russian economy, and widespread gasoline shortages, Russia's dictator may now be fighting not for his nation's security, but for his own skin.
According to a new report in _The Economist_ , Putin has privately told people close to him that "they'll hang me" if he fails to conquer the entire Ukraine Donbas region. The quotation has not been independently confirmed. And it could reflect the usual Kremlin intrigue. But if the quote captures even a fraction of Putin's thinking, it underscores the malignancy of this catastrophe: Putin's disastrous foreign policy adventure has become a test of his own personal survival. Relatedly, he has fewer and fewer reasons to compromise.
Russia's President Putin has built a political system around the proposition that he is indispensable.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/de4e6d95-9dd8-46f2-a099-b904196a4e97?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
He has surrounded himself with flatterers, brutal enforcers, and yes-men. Putin has suppressed dissent, made falling from windows a regular thing, and promoted the image that he alone is the omnipotent czar who can restore Russia to greatness.
For almost five years, Putin has called his invasion of Ukraine a "special military operation," as though a war involving mass casualties, destroyed cities and enormous armies could be made less terrible by giving it the bureaucratic name of a parking violation.

The euphemism has become one of the great jokes of the modern geo-political age--except that the joke has been paid for by Ukrainians and Russians with their lives.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/de4e6d95-9dd8-46f2-a099-b904196a4e97?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
I mentioned the Russian casualties above. Ukraine has suffered an estimated 150,000 military fatalities and another 500 thousand troops wounded. Ukraine has also had more than 20,000 civilians killed by Russia attacks and air strikes.
Vladimir Putin's Kremlin is reportedly considering an even more dangerous escalation. Bloomberg, citing sources close to the Kremlin, reports that Russia is weighing intensified ballistic-missile strikes against Kyiv, potentially including the city center, as well as attacks on infrastructure in other Ukrainian cities. According to the Bloomberg reporting, Moscow does not believe global sanctions on Russia or Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries and logistics networks will persuade Putin to end the war.
This should worry the entire globe.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/de4e6d95-9dd8-46f2-a099-b904196a4e97?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Because the terrifying feature of this moment is not just that Putin is contemplating inflicting more violence. Russia has been contemplating more violence for years. The danger is that Putin's Kremlin seems to increasingly believe that escalation is the only alternative to failure.
[Upgrade to paid](https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly93d3cuYmx1ZWFtcC5jby9zdWJzY3JpYmU_.6LNMiT0QlRN-x3C3yObsO5uQHNv7NsxG5GV_SwRKhhg?&utm_medium=email&utm_source=subscribe-widget&utm_content=213614744)
According to Bloomberg's sources, Putin and his inner circle increasingly regard Ukrainian attacks on Russia as attacks by NATO because alliance members provide Kyiv with weapons and intelligence. If that view hardens, the distinction between a war Russia is fighting against Ukraine and a war Russia believes it is fighting against the West becomes dangerously thin.
And once that distinction disappears, the room for error disappears as well.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/de4e6d95-9dd8-46f2-a099-b904196a4e97?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Also, there does not appear to be any diplomatic exit ramp. Putin reportedly believes he has already made concessions to the U.S. and NATO that weakened Russia's position. Those concessions apparently included promises not to try and kill/decapitate Ukraine's leadership by bombing Ukraine's government center. However, with Russian forces still occupying eastern Ukraine and fighting for more territory, Ukraine has no reason to accept a settlement that rewards aggression.
So, the result is a diplomatic deadlock accompanied by military escalation. That is how wars become traps.
The most disturbing reports concern nuclear weapons.

[https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.

_A third avoidable data mishap under Secretary of State Jena Griswold
exposed sensitive voter records — this time for people who
specifically asked to be shielded from public disclosure._

*
PROTECTED RECORDS EXPOSED FOR 11 DAYS: A routine August 14 update to
Colorado's voter lookup tool inadvertently overrode protections for
voters who requested confidentiality due to safety concerns, exposing
full names, addresses, and other sensitive details until the office
caught the error on August 25 — 59 profiles were accessed before it
was fixed.

*
UNANSWERED QUESTIONS REMAIN: Griswold said she believes the "majority,
but not all" of the 59 searches were confidential voters checking
their own records, but the office has not disclosed how many searches
remain unattributed, by whom, or why.

*
A REPEATING PATTERN: This marks at least the third data-exposure
incident under Griswold's tenure during election years, following a
2024 leak of partial voting-equipment passwords that stayed online for
over four months and a 2022 mailing that sent voter-registration
postcards to roughly 30,000 noncitizens — Griswold is now the
Democratic nominee for attorney general, the office that enforces the
state's data-privacy laws.

recover, and the nearly $32 million his office won from the
e-cigarette maker JUUL. _

number on the ballot, the number in the district’s public materials,
and the figure repeated in news coverage of the measure. The $44
million is not a fixed cap on what the tax could raise in the years
after._

clean_body: This officer was just convicted of manslaughter for trying to stop a fleeing criminal with non-lethal force. | | | | September 01, 2026 | | Tuesday, September 1, 2026 | Estimated Read Time: 3 Minutes Just The Truth Your No-BS Newsletter Dear Readers, Today's sponsored message comes from the Law Enforcement Legal Defense Fund, which is raising tax-deductible donations to fund NYPD Sgt. Erik Duran's appeal after his manslaughter conviction for using a cooler to stop a fleeing suspect. Thank you for your consideration of our sponsors. The Just The Truth Team | Dear Fellow American,This officer was just convicted of manslaughter for trying to stop a fleeing criminal with non-lethal force.Sgt. Erik Duran dedicated 15 years of his life to the NYPD.He earned dozens of commendations. He helped take illegal guns off the streets. He put his life on the line to protect his community.Now he's fighting for his own freedom – All because of a split-second decision he made during a drug bust in the Bronx.| ---|--- An undercover officer had just purchased narcotics from a suspect. As officers moved in to make the arrest, the suspect jumped on a motorized scooter and fled. Duran had only moments to react. He didn't reach for his firearm. He didn't use deadly force. Instead, he grabbed a nearby cooler and threw it into the suspect's path to stop him. The suspect crashed and later died from his injuries. Now, Sgt. Duran has been convicted of manslaughter and sentenced to prison. And he is fighting to clear his name through the appeals process. This appeal is his only chance to avoid spending the next 9 years behind bars with the very criminals he spent his career putting away. The Law Enforcement Legal Defense Fund (LELDF) is standing with Sgt. Duran and helping fund his appeal. But legal battles like this are long, difficult, and incredibly expensive. And while Erik fights for his freedom, his wife and children are left carrying the burden alongside him. They're not only facing the reality of their husband and father spending the next 9 years in prison. Their own lives have been threatened because of this case. That's why I'm asking for your help today. Erik spent 15 years protecting others. Now he needs people like you standing behind him. Thank you for standing with Sgt. Duran. Sincerely, Jason Johnson, President Law Enforcement Legal Defense Fund More such officers who sacrifice so much for will face similar fates unless we speak out and stand up for the brave men and women in blue. subject: Our last primary of the season
disclaimer_text: PAID FOR BY LEADERS WE DESERVE, LEADERSWEDESERVE
body:
We have a real chance to defeat two status quo incumbents today — Patrick and Daniel need our support before the polls close tonight.
# [](https://act.leaderswedeserve.com/go/852?refcode=em20260901-1&t=1&akid=3956%2E587540%2Etps74w)
Today is the day, Peter.
Polls are open right now across Massachusetts, and we have a massive opportunity to replace two status quo incumbents with bold, young, genuine progressive fighters who reflect what the people of their districts deserve: **Patrick Roath** and **Daniel Lander**.
I have been on the ground knocking doors and the energy could not be better. People are fired up and ready for a better Democratic Party. As I was knocking doors with Patrick, multiple voters told us they had received the mailers Leaders We Deserve sent in support of Patrick (the mailers this movement funded!) and they were ecstatic to have a real shot at finally voting out one of the most conservative Democrats in Congress.
Patrick is taking on 25-year incumbent Stephen Lynch, one of the most conservative Democrats in Congress who has voted with Trump multiple times to support ICE, voted against the Affordable Care Act, and taken over $2 million in corporate cash.
At the state level, Daniel is challenging 20-year incumbent William Brownsberger who has repeatedly killed affordable housing bills, backed regressive tax cuts, and fought against unions.
Brownsberger is seen as such a major obstruction to progress in the State Legislature that both Mayor Michelle Wu and Senator Elizabeth Warren have broken with the status quo to endorse Daniel. Yesterday, just after I got off stage at a rally with Daniel, one of his supporters came up to me. She said she was sorry — she'd initially thought the idea of challenging Democratic incumbents was a waste of time, but because of Daniel, she's come around to seeing the value in doing so. She even asked to re-subscribe to our email list!
**On our final primary day, the most important thing I can say to you all is thank you.** When we announced that we wouldn't just be taking on Republicans this cycle, but that we’d also be challenging those Democrats who have failed to meet the moment, many people told us it would be the end of Leaders We Deserve and any future work I could have had in politics. But because of you all, the opposite happened.
We have had the grassroots support to back candidates who will do the right thing, even when that means challenging the status quo. With your help, there have been more retirements from Congress this term than any in the past 100 years. A record number of incumbents have been replaced with true progressive fighters. Young voters are now starting to come back to the Democratic Party because they see themselves and their interests represented in the party.
**This is our last primary day of the cycle, Peter.** I hope that tomorrow morning, I’ll be bringing you good news about their wins — but to make sure we don’t leave anything on the table, we need your support to give Patrick and Daniel a final Election Day push and get them across the finish line.

Thank you,
David Hogg

WE'RE IN THE FINAL STRETCH IN THE COUNTDOWN TO PRIMARY DAY.

DEAR FRIENDS,

It's t-minus 9 days to go, and there are understandably a lot of issues on the minds of voters. I'm invested in solving these
issues for my fellow Rhode Islanders!

Jobs & Workforce is Job One!

For the final nine days, I'd like to talk to you about my Blueprint for Rebuilding Rhode Island and why you so often hear me talk
about "Rhode Island First."

It's because I want you to know that, unlike Seth Magaziner, I understand the challenges life presents when you're not doing well
financially. Growing up tough in Woonsocket where opportunities for good-paying jobs or any at all were few and far between, gives
you an education that you cannot get from an Ivy League ivory tower. People who know me know that I'm often heard to say, 'Good
jobs solve a lot of problems,' because it's true. It's not just the self-esteem of making your own way and providing for your
family that's important. That is important. However, nothing beats being able to buy food & clothes for your family or even
medicine when your kids are sick. Too many politicians know nothing of the hopelessness felt by the underemployed or unemployed
when they cannot afford prescriptions or even food for their families. But... I know that sickening feeling. It doesn't have to be
that way...

The first step to revitalizing our communities is getting workers prepared and ready to join the workforce in two meaningful ways
- ways that will weather the coming storm that will undoubtedly well up as artificial intelligence displaces segments of the
workforce and in the construction-related trades that have been my bread & butter over the last thirty years. Young people and the
moms & dads and grandmothers & grandfathers need to know that I am a builder who knows how to grow those jobs, because I've done
it. I've signed the front of paychecks.

I'll introduce legislation supporting federal workforce development featuring a refocus on the trades during my first days in
Congress, and I'll work across the aisle where necessary to get that passed for our families and our future.

I would be honored to earn your vote. Early voting continues through September 8th, and Primary Day is Wednesday, September 9th.
Every vote matters—make your voice heard.

Thank you for standing with me. Let's get to work!

Sincerely,

Vic Mellor

Candidate for Congress, Rhode Island's 2nd District

clean_body: [] WE'RE IN THE FINAL STRETCH IN THE COUNTDOWN TO PRIMARY DAY. DEAR FRIENDS, It's t-minus 9 days to go, and there are understandably a lot of issues on the minds of voters. I'm invested in solving these issues for my fellow Rhode Islanders! Jobs & Workforce is Job One! For the final nine days, I'd like to talk to you about my Blueprint for Rebuilding Rhode Island and why you so often hear me talk about "Rhode Island First." It's because I want you to know that, unlike Seth Magaziner, I understand the challenges life presents when you're not doing well financially. Growing up tough in Woonsocket where opportunities for good-paying jobs or any at all were few and far between, gives you an education that you cannot get from an Ivy League ivory tower. People who know me know that I'm often heard to say, 'Good jobs solve a lot of problems,' because it's true. It's not just the self-esteem of making your own way and providing for your family that's important. That is important. However, nothing beats being able to buy food & clothes for your family or even medicine when your kids are sick. Too many politicians know nothing of the hopelessness felt by the underemployed or unemployed when they cannot afford prescriptions or even food for their families. But... I know that sickening feeling. It doesn't have to be that way... The first step to revitalizing our communities is getting workers prepared and ready to join the workforce in two meaningful ways - ways that will weather the coming storm that will undoubtedly well up as artificial intelligence displaces segments of the workforce and in the construction-related trades that have been my bread & butter over the last thirty years. Young people and the moms & dads and grandmothers & grandfathers need to know that I am a builder who knows how to grow those jobs, because I've done it. I've signed the front of paychecks. I'll introduce legislation supporting federal workforce development featuring a refocus on the trades during my first days in Congress, and I'll work across the aisle where necessary to get that passed for our families and our future. I would be honored to earn your vote. Early voting continues through September 8th, and Primary Day is Wednesday, September 9th. Every vote matters—make your voice heard. Thank you for standing with me. Let's get to work! Sincerely, Vic Mellor Candidate for Congress, Rhode Island's 2nd District [] [] [] [] [] [] [] Want to change how you receive these emails?

Here’s what’s going on right now in our fight to protect mifepristone access:
→ At the end of last year, the state of Louisiana sued the FDA to try to block this safe, legal medication from being prescribed by telehealth and delivered by mail.
→ After months of back and forth, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in May to allow continued access to mifepristone nationwide while the case proceeds.
Now the case has returned to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit for a merits determination — a ruling on the actual substance of Louisiana’s claim — and I joined a coalition of 23 attorneys general in filing an amicus brief urging the court to issue a final ruling that protects lawful access to mifepristone.
Louisiana’s lawsuit attempts to reinstate a medically unnecessary requirement that mifepristone be dispensed in person — going against decades of scientific evidence.
Reinstating this requirement would create administrative chaos across the country, undermine states’ ability to protect access to reproductive care, and, critically, it would make it more difficult for individuals, especially in rural, low-income, and underserved communities, to access reproductive health care.
Bottom line: mifepristone is a safe, effective, and often lifesaving medication, and attempts to limit access to it are driven by a right-wing, anti-science political movement that’s determined to chip away at reproductive freedom and bodily autonomy nationwide.
I will keep fighting every day to protect reproductive freedom for all, and I want to know if you’re with me. Add your name if you agree that science — not politics — should guide medical decisions. Mifepristone has been FDA-approved for a quarter of a century, and safely used by an estimated 7.5 million people. California will never back down in the fight to protect access to this safe and legal medication, and to ensure medical decisions are made between doctors and patients — not politicians.
Thank you for being here.
—Rob

body:
Different rooms, same energy

Hey Friend, it's Scott Brown with a story to share.

Music has always been part of my life.

Whether I'm on stage with my band or just running through a set in my head between stops, it's how I clear my mind, how I recharge, and how I get ready for whatever the next day on the trail brings.

Last week I spent the day out talking with voters, then closed the night out on stage with my band, guitar in hand, giving it everything I had. Different rooms, same energy. That's just who I am.

[](https://email.alert.republicantaskforce.com/c/eJyckbGunDwQhZ_GdF6Z8f6wFBS_hOhuiihSSmswA1jBgMbji_L2EWivlDrt8fE3c878_HAfGNawzd8wUssyOU7uXFBiTsEL5nmRSDjsWWQJDgxU2jTalA69hE9yTyzGdvQjlr6gtqxfL2hKA3WxtOCtr6epmvwA9j8YxqaBqjR1MwC8KqqL0F4805iybKyB-gHmNT1LMLYm9HVVq6fBlVgeTEce1uBxE0y_pp09Pfwei7VdRI6k7P8KegV9Ip-ZHmfYmMbLcWl-F9ED7-emp531RqdeMB5pCUw6bF5Bf6fVKR_HzqL__oEHXmjb84XmsM3KdsKZFFRZoos0hhyV7Q6KGNa3Kl7Z7vuP3uqvhO-HtGf2pGzHyd3oW_UYDwzzpmz35XfvlWTn3y4NBbfjcYZ1DemuZb6G3RXIP17ts4U_AQAA___ULKrX)

This campaign is a lot like music, actually. It's not something one person can do alone. It takes a chorus. It takes a team. It takes everybody playing their part and showing up, night after night, room after room.

I'm running to fight for the same American Dream I grew up chasing with a single mom, the one I wore a uniform to defend for nearly 40 years, and the one I will never stop believing in for New Hampshire.

**_[But here's the deal. It's going to take all of us working together to get this done and win this primary. If you're ready to join the band, I'd be honored to have you with us.](https://email.alert.republicantaskforce.com/c/eJyckbGunDwQhZ_GdF6Z8f6wFBS_hOhuiihSSmswA1jBgMbji_L2EWivlDrt8fE3c878_HAfGNawzd8wUssyOU7uXFBiTsEL5nmRSDjsWWQJDgxU2jTalA69hE9yTyzGdvQjlr6gtqxfL2hKA3WxtOCtr6epmvwA9j8YxqaBqjR1MwC8KqqL0F4805iybKyB-gHmNT1LMLYm9HVVq6fBlVgeTEce1uBxE0y_pp09Pfwei7VdRI6k7P8KegV9Ip-ZHmfYmMbLcWl-F9ED7-emp531RqdeMB5pCUw6bF5Bf6fVKR_HzqL__oEHXmjb84XmsM3KdsKZFFRZoos0hhyV7Q6KGNa3Kl7Z7vuP3uqvhO-HtGf2pGzHyd3oW_UYDwzzpmz35XfvlWTn3y4NBbfjcYZ1DemuZb6G3RXIP17ts4U_AQAA___ULKrX)_**

body:
